title: Affine neighbourhood pro-scheme of an oriented geometric point
statement:
Let $f:X\to S$ and $g:Y\to S$ be morphisms of schemes [def-pc-scheme], with geometric points $x,y$ [def-weil-geometric-point] and a specialization $c:S_{(g(y))}\to S_{(f(x))}$ of their strict localizations [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit]. Form the left oriented product $P=X_{\mathrm{Et}}\overleftarrow\times_{S_{\mathrm{Et}}}Y_{\mathrm{Et}}$ on its triple site $\mathcal C$ [lem-trf-oriented-product-universal, def-weil-pbc-etale-site], and let $z:\mathbf{Set}\to P$ correspond to $(x,y,c)$. For $T=(U\to V\leftarrow W)$, put $L_z(T)=z^{-1}(h_T^\#)$, where $h_T^\#$ is the sheafification of the representable presheaf [def-weil-pbc-sheafification]. A pointed triple is $(T,a)$ with $a\in L_z(T)$; its morphisms are triple morphisms carrying the chosen element to the chosen element.

The full subcategory $I$ of pointed triples with $U,V,W$ affine is initial in the category of all pointed triples (equivalently, $I^{\mathrm{op}}$ is final for section colimits), is cofiltered, and has a small skeleton [def-weil-size-convention]. The chosen element gives compatible lifts of $x$ to $U$, of $f(x)$ to $V$, and of $y$ to $W$; compatibility means that the image in $V$ of the lift of $y$ is the specialization along $c$ of the image of the lift of $x$.

Set $Z=X\times_SY$ and $D(T,a)=U\times_VW$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. These are affine schemes, are etale over $Z$, and their transition morphisms are affine. The maps from the strict localizations to their neighbourhoods induce a limiting cone of $Z$-schemes
$$M=X_{(x)}\times_{S_{(f(x))}}Y_{(y)}\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \varprojlim_{(T,a)\in I}D(T,a),$$
where $Y_{(y)}\to S_{(f(x))}$ is the composite through $c$. Under this isomorphism the cone maps to $Z$ are the projections from the displayed fibre product. No nonemptiness of $D(T,a)$ or of $M$ is asserted.

source.place: Illusie, Around the Thom--Sebastiani theorem, §1.3, paragraph immediately preceding (1.3.1), printed p. 7; §1.2, inverse image of a triple after (1.2.1), printed p. 5. Read the author PDF in the browser; the copy named by earlier source metadata is absent locally. Oriented site/point conventions corroborated by literature/illusie-laszlo-orgogozo-travaux-de-gabber_arXiv-1207.3648.pdf, Exposé XI, 1.1, 1.6, 1.8.

proof.text:
Write $Q$ for all pointed triples. The inverse-image formula of [lem-trf-oriented-product-universal], applied to $z$, identifies
$$L_z(U\to V\leftarrow W)=x^{-1}(U)\times_{g(y)^{-1}(V)}y^{-1}(W).$$
The first map is the map induced by $U\to f^{-1}V$ followed by the inverse-image mate of $c$, hence has direction $f(x)^{-1}V\to g(y)^{-1}V$. By [lem-galois-stalk-representable], these sets are the geometric lifts. Thus an element is precisely a lift $u$ of $x$ to $U$ and a lift $w$ of $y$ to $W$ such that the image of $w$ in $g(y)^{-1}V$ is $c^\flat(v)$, where $v$ is the image of $u$ in $f(x)^{-1}V$. This also identifies morphisms with the stated pointed triple morphisms, naturally in all three coordinates.

source.place: Exposé XI 1.6, formula (1.a), and 1.8; Stacks sites.tex Tag 00Y6 and etale-cohomology.tex Tag 04FM

proof.text: Use the small site representatives prescribed by [def-weil-size-convention]. The small etale categories have finite limits, and base change preserves them by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-base-change-finite-limits]. Consequently the triple category has componentwise finite limits: structure maps to the base-changed middle coordinate are induced by their universal properties. Apply the cofilteredness assertion of [lem-trf-site-point-fibre] to this site and the point $z$. Its category $\mathcal N_z$ is exactly $Q$, so $Q$ is cofiltered. All categories below are understood through these small representatives.

source.place: Tag 00YA (lemma-point-site-topos), part (2); oriented finite-limit site as in ILO XI 1.1

proof.text: Let $(U\to V\leftarrow W,a)$ be in $Q$, with lifts $(u,v,w)$ as in step 1. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-pointed-etale-neighbourhood-affine-shrink] to choose an affine open $V'\subset V$ containing $v$. Naturality of $c^\flat$ under the open immersion $V'\to V$ shows that the specialization of $v$ lifts to $V'$; its image in $V$ is the image of $w$. Therefore $u$ lies in the open inverse image of $V'$ in $U$, and $w$ lies in the open inverse image of $V'$ in $W$. Apply the same affine-shrink lemma to those two open subsets, obtaining affine opens $U'\subset U$, $W'\subset W$ containing the lifts and mapping to $V'$. The lifted elements still satisfy the equation of step 1, since both are the restrictions of the given elements and an open immersion has at most one lift of a geometric point. Thus $(U'\to V'\leftarrow W',a')$ is in $I$ and maps to the original pointed triple. This uses only open neighbourhoods of the chosen points, with no separatedness or quasi-separatedness hypothesis.

source.place: Exposé XI 1.6 and 1.8; affine refinement in Illusie §1.3 before (1.3.1); Stacks etale-cohomology.tex Tag 04HX, affine-neighbourhood refinement

proof.text: The inclusion $I\subset Q$ is full and every object of $Q$ receives an arrow from $I$ by step 3. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-colimit-initial-full-subcategory](1): $I$ is cofiltered and restriction along $I^{\mathrm{op}}\to Q^{\mathrm{op}}$ preserves section colimits. For completeness, the initiality comma category over $q\in Q$ is nonempty by step 3. Given two of its objects, take a common predecessor in $Q$, then equalize its two maps to $q$ by cofilteredness, and refine the resulting object by step 3; this gives a predecessor in the comma category. Hence that comma category is connected and $I\to Q$ is initial. In the size convention of [def-weil-size-convention], triples form a small category and each $L_z(T)$ is a set; the union of these sets of pointed objects and of the sets of pointed arrows is small in the containing universe. Passing back from representatives gives the claimed small skeleton.

source.place: Definition definition-initial and dual of Tag 04E7; full-subcategory criterion

proof.text:
For an affine triple, [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] identifies $D(T,a)$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(\Gamma(U)\otimes_{\Gamma(V)}\Gamma(W))$, so it is affine. Any transition is consequently affine by [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-affine-schemes-affine]. To check etaleness over $Z$, first $Y\times_SV\to Y$ is etale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change]. The structural map $W\to Y\times_SV$ is etale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-composition-cancellation](3), since both its source and target are etale over $Y$. Its base change by $U\times_SY\to Y\times_SV$ is
$$U\times_VW\longrightarrow U\times_SY,$$
so is etale. The map $U\times_SY\to X\times_SY=Z$ is the base change of $U\to X$, so is etale as well. Their composite is etale by the composition assertion of the same cancellation node. Triple morphisms induce morphisms of these fibre products by their defining projections; the identities and compositions follow from uniqueness in the fibre-product universal property [def-pc-fibre-product].

Let $H_U,H_V,H_W$ send an object of $I$ to its pointed affine neighbourhood of $x,f(x),y$, respectively, using step 1 and the category of [def-weil-pbc-pointed-etale-neighbourhoods]. Each target object receives a map from a projected triple. Indeed, for $(U_0,u_0)$ use the pointed triple $(U_0\to S\leftarrow Y)$; for $(W_0,w_0)$ use $(X\to S\leftarrow W_0)$. For $(V_0,v_0)$ use
$$(X\times_SV_0\to V_0\leftarrow Y\times_SV_0),$$
with lifts $(x,v_0)$ and $(y,c^\flat(v_0))$. These are objects of the etale triple site by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change], and they are pointed by the equation of step 1. Apply step 3 to each prototype to obtain an object of $I$ and the required pointed map from its coordinate to the given target neighbourhood.

source.place: Exposé XI 1.6 and 1.8; explicit coordinate refinements underlying Illusie §1.3 before (1.3.1)

proof.text:
Check the equalization condition for the three coordinate functors. For parallel pointed maps $s,s':U\to U_0$, take their equalizer $E\to U$ in $X_{\mathrm{Et}}$ using [lem-weil-pbc-etale-base-change-finite-limits]. Since the maps agree on the chosen lift of $x$, that lift factors through $E$; replace the triple by $(E\to V\leftarrow W)$ and refine it using step 3. Its arrow to the original triple equalizes $s,s'$ on the $U$ coordinate. The same construction on $W$ treats $H_W$. For parallel pointed maps $s,s':V\to V_0$, take their equalizer $E\to V$ in $S_{\mathrm{Et}}$ and replace the triple by
$$(U\times_VE\to E\leftarrow W\times_VE).$$
The lift $v$ factors through $E$; naturality of $c^\flat$ gives the compatible factorization of the image of $w$. Thus the triple is pointed. Its outside coordinates are etale over $X,Y$: $E\to V$ is a morphism of etale $S$-schemes, hence etale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-composition-cancellation](3); now apply [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change] and composition. Affinely refine this triple by step 3. The resulting arrow equalizes $s,s'$ on the middle coordinate.

source.place: Exposé XI 1.6, functorial fibre formula; Stacks topologies.tex Tag 021D and morphisms.tex Tags 02GO, 02GW, 02GN

proof.text:
Steps 6 and 7 are precisely conditions (i) and (ii) of [lem-weil-pbc-initial-functor-cofiltered-criterion](1). Since $I$ is cofiltered, all three coordinate functors are initial. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-initial-functor-limit] to the diagrams that forget the chosen geometric lift. The inverse-limit characterization in [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit] then gives, with their canonical cone maps,
$$\varprojlim_I U=X_{(x)},\qquad \varprojlim_I V=S_{(f(x))},\qquad \varprojlim_I W=Y_{(y)}.$$
The definition uses small skeletons; equivalences of representative categories preserve the same limit cones, as included in that definition. Therefore the limit-invariance lemma is applied to actual small diagrams, without assuming any Noetherian, separation, or finite-type condition on $f$ or $g$.

source.place: Tag 04E7 and its dual; Tag 002R (lemma-initial); strict-local neighbourhood limits in etale-cohomology.tex Tag 04HX

proof.text: Under the three limit identifications of step 8, the maps $U\to V$ induce the natural map $X_{(x)}\to S_{(f(x))}$: for every $(V_0,v_0)$ the prototype of step 6 gives the component obtained by projecting the pointed neighbourhood $X\times_SV_0$ to $V_0$. The maps $W\to V$ induce $Y_{(y)}\to S_{(g(y))}\xrightarrow{c}S_{(f(x))}$: the component at $(V_0,v_0)$ is the projection to $V_0$ belonging to the pointed $Y$-neighbourhood $(Y\times_SV_0,(y,c^\flat(v_0)))$. This is exactly the component prescribed by $c$ on that etale neighbourhood, because $c^\flat$ is its inverse-image mate in [lem-trf-oriented-product-universal]. The limit projections in [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit] determine a map uniquely, so these component checks identify the maps themselves, not just their values at closed points. For any other triple mapping to the prototype, the component equation follows from its two structural maps, and step 8 makes it independent of the chosen refinement.

source.place: Exposé XI 1.6 and 1.8, maps of points in inverse-image convention; Illusie §1.3, description of the map through c

proof.text: Put $A=X_{(x)}$, $B=S_{(f(x))}$ and $C=Y_{(y)}$, with the maps identified in step 9. The fibre product $M=A\times_BC$ [def-pc-fibre-product] gives compatible maps to every $U\times_VW$: its two components are the canonical projections $M\to A\to U$ and $M\to C\to W$, which agree in $V$ by step 9. Conversely, a cone with arbitrary scheme vertex $R$ on $D$ gives compatible maps $R\to U$, $R\to W$ and their common composite $R\to V$. The three limiting cones of step 8 give unique maps $R\to A$, $R\to C$, $R\to B$. The first two agree in $B$, since their composites with every projection $B\to V$ are that common component. Thus there is a unique $R\to A\times_BC$, whose compositions with the cone maps recover the given cone. Uniqueness follows from uniqueness in the limits of $U,W$ and in the fibre product. This proves the asserted limit isomorphism. Each cone map to $Z$ has coordinates $M\to A\to X$ and $M\to C\to Y$, so the isomorphism is over $Z$. The argument also works for $M=\varnothing$ and for empty stages; it never constructs a point of any fibre product.
